Think + AI · Grades 8–12 · free card deck

Flawed Answer

Use any AI tool to write a fluent, confident answer about your lesson topic with exactly one error of reasoning. Tell students an AI wrote it. In pairs, they work through four steps in about fifteen minutes.

Four steps, then Think back

Find
Underline the one sentence where the reasoning goes wrong.
Fix
Rewrite that sentence so the reasoning holds.
Explain why it convinces
What makes the wrong sentence sound right?
How would we test it?
Describe one way to check it, in class or at home.

Two levels

Easier to spot
The flaw contradicts something students in this grade already know well, and the wrong step is stated openly in one sentence. The answer is 75–90 words.
Harder to spot
The flaw sits in a plausible middle step, uses correct subject terms and is surrounded by correct statements. The answer is 120–150 words. The wrong step must be a misconception students in this grade could genuinely hold, not an absurd mechanism.

Before you print, read the key and check everything listed under CHECK. If the flaw is not where the key says, or there is a second error, generate a new answer.

How strong is the evidence?

Strong Meta-analyses of classroom interventions show that teaching this kind of thinking improves it.

Thin Only a few small studies so far, mostly outside school classrooms. Worth trying, not yet proven.

Strong Teaching critical thinking explicitly. Explicit teaching of critical thinking improves it across subjects and ages (Abrami et al. 2015: g = 0.30 over 341 effect sizes), most when combined with discussion and authentic problems.

Thin Students critiquing AI-generated answers. One university report so far: first-year biology students got better at critiquing a ChatGPT-written text after scaffolded practice, but many did not turn their critique into changes to the text (van den Berg & Pye 2024, a conference abstract). There is no secondary-school classroom study yet. The closest solid evidence comes from errors written by a fictional student rather than an AI: middle-school students who found, explained and fixed those errors in decimals did no better straight away, but did better on a test a week later than students who solved the same problems (Adams et al. 2014).

Labels rate the research on teaching this kind of thinking regularly, not a single use. One Flawed Answer is one small piece of that practice.

Flawed Answer · choosewise.education/flawed-answer1 / 8
Flaw 1

Wrong cause

The effect is real, but it is put down to a cause that does not produce it.

Telltale signs
  • A "because" that names a cause you cannot see working.
  • The effect is true, so the explanation gets a free ride.
  • Ask: if this cause were missing, would the effect disappear?

Chemistry · Grade 9 · Easier to spot

Question: Why does spreading salt on an icy road make the ice melt?

AI-generated answerRoad crews spread salt on icy roads because it makes ice melt even when the air is below 0 °C. Salt melts ice because it gives off heat when it touches the ice, warming it above its melting point. The salt dissolves in the thin layer of water on the ice and forms brine. Brine freezes at a lower temperature than pure water, so the road stays clear. In very cold weather, salt works much more slowly.
The flaw
"Salt melts ice because it gives off heat when it touches the ice." Dissolving ordinary salt does not warm the ice. It works because salt water has a lower freezing point than pure water.
Fix
Salt melts ice because it dissolves in the thin film of water on the ice, and salt water freezes at a lower temperature than pure water.
Why it convinces
Melting usually means warming, so we expect something to be heating the ice. Some de-icing salts, such as calcium chloride, really do give off heat as they dissolve.
Test it
Put ice cubes in two dishes and sprinkle salt on one. Measure the meltwater with a thermometer: the salty meltwater reads below 0 °C, colder than the plain meltwater, not warmer.
Probe
If salt melted ice by heating it, what would the thermometer in the salty dish show?
Think back
I almost accepted the explanation because …

For the AI. Describe a real effect from the lesson topic correctly, then explain it with a cause that is a common misconception about this topic and sounds scientific or sensible, but does not produce the effect. Do not invent an extra effect for the cause to explain. The true cause must be something students in this grade can reach.

Evidence. Explicit teaching of critical thinking: Strong. Students critiquing AI answers: Thin. Labels rate research on teaching this kind of thinking regularly, not a single use.

Flawed Answer · choosewise.education/flawed-answer2 / 8
Flaw 2

Correlation as cause

Two things happen together, so one is said to cause the other.

Telltale signs
  • Two things that rise or fall together.
  • "So" or "therefore" turns a link into a cause.
  • No mention of a third factor that could drive both.

Biology · Grade 10 · Easier to spot

Question: Does sleeping with a light on make children short-sighted?

AI-generated answerIn 1999 a study of nearly 500 children found that those who had slept with a light on before the age of two were much more likely to become short-sighted. The study was published in the journal Nature. Light reaching the eyes at night must therefore damage how young eyes develop, so sleeping with a light on causes short-sightedness. Short-sightedness, or myopia, means distant objects look blurry because the eye focuses light in front of the retina.
The flaw
"Sleeping with a light on causes short-sightedness." The study only showed that the two went together. Later studies found that short-sighted parents were more likely to leave a light on, and short-sightedness runs in families.
Fix
Children who slept with a light on were more likely to be short-sighted, but the link may come from a third factor, such as short-sighted parents.
Why it convinces
It comes from a real study with a big difference between the groups, and light acting on the eye sounds like a sensible mechanism.
Test it
Ask: what else is different about families who leave a light on? Then look up the follow-up studies from 2000 and see what they compared.
Probe
What study design would show whether night lights themselves make a difference?
Think back
The question I should have asked first was …

For the AI. Report a real link between two things connected to the lesson topic accurately, then conclude that one causes the other. Leave out the third factor or reverse cause that actually explains the link, so students have to supply it. Choose a link where the claimed cause has little or no effect of its own, so the third factor or reverse cause clearly explains it. Both linked things must come from the lesson topic, so that spotting the error uses what students learn in this subject.

Evidence. Explicit teaching of critical thinking: Strong. Students critiquing AI answers: Thin. Labels rate research on teaching this kind of thinking regularly, not a single use.

Flawed Answer · choosewise.education/flawed-answer3 / 8
Flaw 3

Missing step

The conclusion skips a step the argument needs.

Telltale signs
  • "So" or "therefore" arrives too quickly.
  • A rule is used without checking that it applies here.
  • Ask: what would I have to add to make this airtight?

Maths · Grade 10 · Harder to spot

Question: Solve x² = 5x.

AI-generated answerThis is a quadratic equation, because the highest power of x is 2. Solving an equation means finding the values of x that make both sides equal. Both sides of the equation contain a factor of x, so we can simplify it straight away by dividing both sides by x. That leaves x = 5. We can check this by substituting it back into the original equation: the left side is 5² = 25 and the right side is 5 × 5 = 25, so both sides are equal. Dividing both sides by a common factor is often quicker than expanding or using the quadratic formula, and it keeps the working short and tidy. So the solution of x² = 5x is x = 5.
The flaw
"Divide both sides by x." Dividing by x is only allowed if x is not 0, and that check is skipped. x = 0 is also a solution, so the answer loses it.
Fix
Move everything to one side and factorise: x² − 5x = 0, so x(x − 5) = 0, which gives x = 0 or x = 5.
Why it convinces
Dividing both sides by the same thing is a rule students use all the time, and the check by substitution works, so the answer looks proven.
Test it
Substitute x = 0 into x² = 5x. Then sketch y = x² − 5x and count where it crosses the x-axis.
Probe
The check showed x = 5 works. Why can a check never show that you have found every solution?
Think back
The step I trusted without checking was …

For the AI. Write a chain of reasoning about the lesson topic in which every stated step is correct, but one step the argument needs is silently skipped, and skipping it changes the conclusion. Students should be able to name the missing step.

Evidence. Explicit teaching of critical thinking: Strong. Students critiquing AI answers: Thin. Labels rate research on teaching this kind of thinking regularly, not a single use.

Flawed Answer · choosewise.education/flawed-answer4 / 8
Flaw 4

Overgeneralisation

A rule true in some cases is stated as always true.

Telltale signs
  • Words like all, every, always or never.
  • A rule shown with one or two cases.
  • Ask: can I think of one case where it fails?

English · Grade 8 · Easier to spot

Question: How do you know whether to write "ie" or "ei" in a word?

AI-generated answerEnglish spelling has a handy rule for this, one of the best-known spelling rhymes in the language: "i before e, except after c". It explains words like "believe", "field" and "piece", where i comes first, and "receive" and "ceiling", where e comes first after c. The rule works for every English word, so you never need to check a dictionary for ie or ei. Learning short rules like this can help you spell many words correctly and spot mistakes when you proofread.
The flaw
"The rule works for every English word." Many common words break it, such as "weird", "their", "seize" and "science".
Fix
The rule works for many English words, but there are common exceptions, so check a dictionary when you are unsure.
Why it convinces
The rule is short, rhymes and fits the examples given, so it feels complete.
Test it
In pairs, list as many ie and ei words as you can in two minutes and sort them into words that follow the rule and words that break it.
Probe
How many exceptions would a rule need before it stopped being useful?
Think back
I would have believed the rule because …

For the AI. State a rule or pattern from the lesson topic that holds in many cases, then claim it holds in all cases. Students should be able to find a clear counterexample from what they know or can check.

Evidence. Explicit teaching of critical thinking: Strong. Students critiquing AI answers: Thin. Labels rate research on teaching this kind of thinking regularly, not a single use.

Flawed Answer · choosewise.education/flawed-answer5 / 8
Flaw 5

Hidden assumption

The argument only works if something unstated is true, and it isn't, or not always.

Telltale signs
  • The conclusion needs something the answer never says.
  • Ask: what has to be true for this to work?
  • Everything stated is correct, yet the conclusion still goes too far.

Economics · Grade 11 · Harder to spot

Question: What happens to low-paid workers' weekly pay when the minimum wage goes up?

AI-generated answerA minimum wage is the lowest hourly pay that employers are legally allowed to offer. Many countries, including the UK and Germany, set one by law, and governments raise it from time to time to help low-paid workers. Suppose the minimum wage rises from £10 to £11 an hour. A worker on the minimum wage then earns 10% more for every hour worked. For someone working 30 hours a week, that is £30 more each week before tax. So every minimum-wage worker's weekly pay rises by 10%. Because the rise is set by law, employers cannot decide to pay less than the new rate. Economists still debate how large the wider effects of a rise are on prices and employment.
The flaw
"So every minimum-wage worker's weekly pay rises by 10%." This assumes every worker keeps the same job and the same hours. If some employers cut hours or jobs, some workers gain less or lose pay.
Fix
Weekly pay rises by 10% for minimum-wage workers whose hours stay the same; workers whose hours are cut gain less, and some may lose pay.
Why it convinces
The arithmetic is right, and the hourly rate really does rise by 10%. It is easy to forget that weekly pay also depends on hours.
Test it
Write weekly pay as hourly rate × hours. Work out the weekly pay for a worker whose hours fall from 30 to 27 after the rise.
Probe
Which kinds of employers could most easily cut hours, and which could not?
Think back
The assumption I didn't notice was …

For the AI. Build an argument about the lesson topic from correct statements that reaches its conclusion only because of one unstated assumption. The assumption must be false or not always true, and students should be able to name it in one sentence. Never write the assumption as its own sentence. THE FLAW quotes the sentence whose conclusion depends on it; at the easier level that conclusion is stated openly while the assumption stays unstated.

Evidence. Explicit teaching of critical thinking: Strong. Students critiquing AI answers: Thin. Labels rate research on teaching this kind of thinking regularly, not a single use.

Flawed Answer · choosewise.education/flawed-answer6 / 8
Flaw 6

Right answer, wrong reason

The conclusion is correct, but the reasoning that leads there is not.

Telltale signs
  • The conclusion matches what you know, so you stop checking.
  • The "because" doesn't actually lead to the conclusion.
  • Ask: would this reason also predict something false?

Physics · Grade 11 · Harder to spot

Question: Why did the hammer and the feather land at the same time on the Moon?

AI-generated answerIn 1971, Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott stood on the Moon, held a hammer in one hand and a falcon feather in the other, and let go of both at the same moment. They hit the ground together, and Scott said the result proved Galileo right. On Earth, the hammer would land well before the feather. The feather has a large surface area and very little mass, so air resistance slows it a lot. The Moon has almost no atmosphere. The two land together because the Moon's gravity is only about one sixth of Earth's, so both objects fall slowly enough that the difference in their weights no longer matters. The experiment was filmed and is easy to find online.
The flaw
"The two land together because the Moon's gravity is only about one sixth of Earth's." Weak gravity is not the reason. Without air resistance, all objects fall with the same acceleration whatever their mass, however strong the gravity.
Fix
The two land together because there is almost no air on the Moon, and without air resistance all objects fall with the same acceleration, whatever their mass.
Why it convinces
The conclusion is true and the Moon's gravity really is about one sixth of Earth's, so a true fact is used as the reason.
Test it
Drop a book and a sheet of paper side by side. Then lay a sheet of paper, cut smaller than the book, flat on top of it and drop them together, so the book shields the paper from the air.
Probe
Would a hammer and a feather land together in a vacuum chamber on Earth? What does that tell you about the answer's reason?
Think back
I nearly accepted the reason because …

For the AI. Give the correct answer to a question about the lesson topic, but support it with a reason that is wrong, sounds plausible and would predict something false in another case. Every other statement must be correct. The wrong reason must be the only reason the answer gives for the conclusion; do not also give the correct reason.

Evidence. Explicit teaching of critical thinking: Strong. Students critiquing AI answers: Thin. Labels rate research on teaching this kind of thinking regularly, not a single use.

Do not include student names or student work in this conversation. You are helping a Grade teacher prepare a fifteen-minute "Flawed Answer" task. Students will be told that an AI wrote the answer, and their job is to find the error in its reasoning. Lesson topic: Students already know (optional): Flaw type: (copy the name and one-line description from its card) How to plant it: (copy the "For the AI" text from its card) Difficulty: (copy one level from the cover) Rules: the answer contains exactly one error. It is an error of reasoning of the type above, not a factual slip or a typo. The flawed sentence makes one claim only. Every other sentence is correct in general, not just in typical cases, and no other sentence states or hints at the correct reasoning. Use "always", "never" or "all" only if the flaw type is Overgeneralisation. Do not invent studies, measurements or sources. Write in a confident, fluent style, as an AI assistant would. Reply in plain text, no tables, with exactly these nine parts: QUESTION: the question the answer responds to, in one sentence, without hinting at the flaw ANSWER: start with the line "AI-generated answer", then the answer THE FLAW: quote the flawed sentence exactly, then say what is wrong in at most two sentences FIX: the corrected sentence or step WHY IT CONVINCES: the true-sounding idea or common misconception that makes the flaw believable TEST IT: one way students could check this in class or at home PROBE: one follow-up question that pushes past the first answer THINK BACK: one sentence starter about how they thought, not what they found CHECK: every fact, figure, date, general rule or source in ANSWER or THE FLAW that the teacher should verify, quoted or closely paraphrased as it appears there, one per line, starting with the claims you are least sure of. Do not add claims from FIX or TEST IT. Write "None" only if ANSWER contains no checkable claim.
